extraction.name: DocVQA
extraction.description: A dataset for visual question answering on document images, comprising 50,000 questions and answers over 12,767 images drawn from 6,071 industry documents. Documents include varied types, layouts, and typewritten, printed, handwritten, and born-digital text. Questions are tagged with one or more of nine question types.
extraction.creator: Minesh Mathew; Dimosthenis Karatzas; C. V. Jawahar
extraction.citeAs: Minesh Mathew, Dimosthenis Karatzas, and C. V. Jawahar. DocVQA: A Dataset for VQA on Document Images. arXiv:2007.00398v3, 5 January 2021.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors downloaded documents from different collections in the UCSF Industry Documents Library and manually selected pages. They tried to minimize binarized images to avoid poor image quality becoming a bottleneck and prioritized pages containing tables, forms, lists, and figures over pages containing only running text. Questions and answers were collected from remote workers through a three-stage annotation process.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The year-wise distribution of source documents includes a category labeled '<date not known>'.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Document images were sourced from the UCSF Industry Documents Library (https://www.industrydocuments.ucsf.edu/). The selected pages come from 6,071 documents across tobacco, food, drug, fossil fuel, and chemical industries. Documents with known dates range from 1900 to 2018, mostly from 1960–2000. Many documents were selected from food and nutrition collections because these contained a good number of non-binarized images.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was randomly divided into training, validation, and test splits in an 80:10:10 ratio. Training contains 39,463 questions and 10,194 images; validation contains 5,349 questions and 1,286 images; testing contains 5,188 questions and 1,287 images.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions flagged during verification for language issues or ambiguity were excluded. OCR tokens were extracted using a commercial OCR application for dataset analysis and baseline experiments. For BERT fine-tuning, OCR tokens were serialized into a space-separated string in top-left to bottom-right order. Data were converted into SQuAD-style format, with answer spans approximated using the first match of the answer string in the serialized OCR text.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: In stage 1, remote workers viewed a document image and authored at most 10 question-answer pairs. They were instructed to ask questions answerable using text in the image and to copy answers verbatim. Multiple ground-truth answers were encouraged when warranted, and documents could be skipped if questions could not be framed. In stage 2, workers independently answered the questions without seeing stage-1 answers, assigned one or more question types, and could flag unsuitable questions. The nine types are handwritten, form, layout, table/list, other, running text, photograph, figure, and yes/no. Questions with no exact answer agreement between stages 1 and 2 were reviewed by the authors in stage 3, where questions and answers could be edited or additional answers added before acceptance or rejection.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A web-based annotation tool supporting question-answer collection, independent answer verification, question-type tagging, flagging, and author review.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Answers from the first and second annotation stages were compared using exact matching. If no answer from one stage matched any answer from the other, the question was sent to the authors for review. Authors could edit questions and answers, add answers, accept the item, or reject it. Questions flagged as unsuitable because of language issues or ambiguity were excluded. Multiple ground-truth answers and multiple question-type labels were permitted.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each retained question underwent two answer-annotation stages, with an additional author-review stage when the answers did not match exactly. Multiple answers could be entered per question; a fixed number of final answers per question is not specified.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: An unnamed commercial OCR application was used to extract text tokens from document images for analysis and baseline experiments.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Answers include names of people and places. Examples contain personal names, a passenger's name, addresses, ZIP codes, and a telephone extension number.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The selection favored non-binarized images and pages containing tables, forms, lists, and figures rather than only running text. Many documents came from food and nutrition collections because they offered non-binarized images. Most documents date from 1960–2000. Questions repeatedly ask about dates, titles, and page numbers, and almost all of the most frequent answers are numeric values.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Binarization in the source library reduced image quality, motivating efforts to minimize such images in the dataset. OCR errors, including over-segmentation, can prevent correct answers even when models identify the relevant image region. The paper reports a large gap between baseline model performance and human performance, particularly for questions requiring document structure, figures, diagrams, text on photographs, or handwriting recognition.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, testing, and fine-tuning of visual question answering and extractive question answering models on document images. The dataset supports evaluating document understanding using textual content, layout, tables, forms, figures, and other visual cues, including performance analysis by question type. The paper evaluates LoRRA, M4C, and BERT baselines and uses Average Normalized Levenshtein Similarity as the primary evaluation metric to avoid severely penalizing minor answer differences caused by OCR errors.
